newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda adjourns genocide trials, more announced.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda adjourns genocide trials, more announced.

text.p: Two Rwandans appeared in court on Monday for the first genocide trials in the Rwandan capital but their cases were immediately adjourned.
Deputy justice minister Gerard Gahima later announced that more genocide trials would take place on Tuesday in the northeastern city of Byumba.
One of the suspects was named as Francois Bizimana while the other was said to be a former speaker of Rwanda's parliament whose name was not immediately known.
A court in Kigali adjourned the trial of Silas Munyageshali, a former prosecutor in Kigali, to an unnamed date in 1997 and the case was moved to the town of Gitarama south of Kigali.
A three-man panel of judges headed by Judge Juriel Rutaremara ruled that it would be unfair to try Munyageshali in the same court he previously served as prosecutor.
The trial of Theodomir Ruzirabwoba, a 50-year-old former administrator in Kigali, was adjourned until January 3 to allow victims' counsel more time to compile evidence against him.

Ruzirabwoba is accused of overseeing the massacres of minority Tutsis living in an area under his control at that time, of not preventing genocide, and of personally killing those targetted during the slaughter.

"He carried out killings with the assistance of at least two others. He did nothing to stop the killings and oversaw them being carried out in the area under his jurisdiction," said prosecuting magistrate Pascal Kalisa.
Both men were not asked to enter a plea.
Faoduald Karamira, a prominent politician and former second vice-president of the Hutu MDR/Power party, did not appear in court as had been expected. No explanation was given.
Karamira was a senior official of the extremist Interahamwe Hutu militia, accused of playing a leading role in the genocide in 1994 that killed hundreds of thousands of Tutsis.
He was accused of speaking regularly on the Radio Mille Collines and Rwanda Radio, urging Hutus to slaughter rival Tutsi tribes people.

The first genocide trials in Rwanda opened on Friday in the southeastern town of Kibungo, where Deo Bizimana, a former medical assistant, and Egide Gatanazi, a former local administrator, both pleaded not guilty to organising massacres.
Those convicted on charges of taking part in the 1994 slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis along with Hutu moderates face the death penalty after one chance of appeal.
Deputy justice minister Gahima told reporters that the government was contemplating public executions of those found guilty.
In the Kenyan capital Nairobi, a Hutu refugee lobby group -- the Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy in Rwanda (RDR) -- dismissed Rwanda's judicial move as "Kangaroo trials".

"In an effort to hoodwink the world that there is a semblance of sanity in the judicial system in Rwanda, the government has launched Kangaroo trials whereby a suspect is convicted before trial," an RDR statement said.

The RDR said suspects had recieved no legal counselling of their choice and had been denied the right to be tried in languages of their choice by the English-speaking administration that overthrew a French system.
